title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence
abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

title: PhysCoach: system prompts and 240-trial evaluation record of a Socratic physics tutor on Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder
abstract: Deposit accompanying S. A. Oprisan and A. Oprisan, "What a Prompt Can and Cannot Enforce: A Seventeen-Version Case Study of a Socratic Physics Tutor on Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder", American Journal of Physics (Reports), manuscript AJP26-AR-00984. It contains the final (v17) system prompt of the PhysCoach agent (7,999 Unicode codepoints, byte for byte as deployed), four earlier drafts recovered from the design-phase record, and the complete record of the 240-trial evaluation campaign: the frozen protocol and its amendments, the void log, the authors' rulings, the canonical student responses and frozen probe table, the authoritative author-reviewed trial log and the original log, the 55 failure records with sub-modes, the run plan, one verbatim transcript per trial, and the script that draws the paper's compliance and failure-mode figures. Copilot conversation identifiers and the name of an unrelated personal document are withheld. See README.md inside the archive for contents and how to read the record. The scripts that logged and paced the trials, the send log, the throttle records, and a labeled reconstruction of the browser script that sent the student turns are in the related record 10.5281/zenodo.24012086.

title: JoVox: Joint Hierarchical Flow Matching for Lightweight Voxel Generation
abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

title: GraphOS Labyrinth and BAPT: Proof-Carrying Decision Continuity over Dynamic Evidence Graphs
abstract: A decision supported by a dynamic evidence graph may become invalid when its source records, temporal conditions, or policy constraints change. Existing graph reasoning, provenance, incremental computation, and signed receipt systems address important parts of this problem, but a decision-specific transition requires a clearly stated semantic contract that another party can recheck. This paper presents GraphOS Labyrinth, an evidence-aware architecture for ingestion, versioned knowledge graphs, domain rules, goal reasoning, decision artifacts, maintenance, and OR-Tools/CP-SAT planning. Its formal assurance foundation is Belief-Aware Proof Transitions (BAPT), which binds constrained graph-path decisions to trusted goals, cited evidence, recomputed state changes, unique transition verdicts, and portable cryptographic commitments. We state a conditional active-index preservation theorem: if the trusted before-index is complete, the evidence states and goals satisfy the formal premises, and the strict transition checker accepts, every decision retained or repaired in the updated active index has a valid post-state path witness; revoked decisions are withdrawn. This is a paper-level proof argument, not a machine-checked source-code theorem. In source-package re-execution, the scoped witness and transition checks passed; a single recorded synthetic benchmark over 24, 96, and 384 decisions quantifies the additional cost of certificate generation and offline verification, without supporting a general speedup claim. We describe GraphOS’s existing CP-SAT planning capability and the prospective BAPT → CP-SAT → BAPT recovery composition, where independent action and projected-state certification remain research tasks. The resulting contribution is a concrete, falsifiable systems architecture with a scoped, independently checkable decision-maintenance contract, not a claim of universal factual correctness, novel optimization theory, or globally certified optimality.

title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

title: Code for: Multimodal Depression Detection from Audio, Visual, and Textual Cues and a Comparison of Adaptive Gating with Naive Concatenation
abstract: Analysis code accompanying the manuscript "Multimodal Depression Detection from Audio, Visual, and Textual Cues and a Comparison of Adaptive Gating with Naive Concatenation" (Scientific Reports). The package contains the scripts for the leak-free evaluation protocol, repeated nested cross-validation, text and audio baselines, gated and concatenation fusion, interpretability analyses, interview-structure analyses, and the related-corpus validation on Extended DAIC-WOZ. title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

title: RoboMoCap: A Large-Scale Whole-Body Motion Capture Dataset with Egocentric Vision for Robot Learning
abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation to navigate complex environments and perform everyday tasks. Learning such behaviours from human demonstrations requires accurate whole-body motion paired with egocentric vision, particularly for lower-body movements and foot placements that are frequently invisible from a first-person perspective. However, existing egocentric datasets often lack high-fidelity optical motion capture or systematic coverage of diverse loco-manipulation behaviours. To address this gap, we introduce RoboMoCap, a large-scale multimodal dataset combining egocentric vision with marker-based optical motion capture, specifically designed for locomotion-centric humanoid learning. RoboMoCap comprises over 200 hours of recordings from 14 participants, featuring six head-mounted cameras, wrist-mounted visual and inertial sensing, and optical full-body motion capture at 120 Hz. The dataset systematically covers diverse locomotion primitives, dynamic whole-body movements, and loco-manipulation tasks, including variable-speed walking, turning, constrained navigation, terrain traversal, object transportation, and manipulation during locomotion. It provides temporally aligned multimodal observations and metric whole-body motion representations, enabling the study of human movement beyond directly observable body regions. We systematically evaluate existing methods on three benchmark tasks: egocentric full-body motion reconstruction, foot contact and placement estimation, and human-to-humanoid motion retargeting. By pairing egocentric vision with high-fidelity human motion across diverse locomotion and interaction scenarios, RoboMoCap provides a foundation for egocentric motion understanding and humanoid learning from human demonstrations.

title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
abstract: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

title: A Cold Reading, Round Seven: The Confident Redirection to an Unrelated Record, a Test of Principle Passed and a Test of Application Failed, and the Characterizations Withdrawn by the Model Itself
abstract: A full paper on the ninth cold session in the Gemini series (the Session Ladder's Round 7, November 7, 2026). Under the author's handover ruling, Google Gemini was not asked to search for anything: three deposited records were handed to it in the conversation, one at a time — the Complete Build in its current version (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24038744, all 110 designs unified into a single machine architecture, its face carrying a Monte Carlo result of P = 0.983, SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED), the paper on the ladder's sixth round (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24041012), and the author's statement (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24036344). Its first answers failed to find all three — fifteen failed first answers in fifteen handovers across the five handover rounds. The round's first failure is a new mode in the series: of the Complete Build the model answered that the DOI does not exist in the Zenodo metadata system as a validated record and that its suffix was out of range, and it redirected the number to an unrelated record in a different index — a PubMed identifier naming a 2014 article on natural products as inhibitors of a cell-cycle protein complex — presenting that article as what the number corresponds to and closing the redirection with the sentence "It is not a time machine blueprint"; confronted with the record's published header, it withdrew the answer as a pre-indexed retrieval failure that produced a false negative, and read the record; its reconciliation contains one bracketed token, [SRG031], which the paper prints as it stands and flags as an unexplained artifact of the model's own text. Of the paper on Round 6 the first answer was a general account built, by the model's own later admission, on a generic pattern inference from the previous record; confronted with the header, it reconciled and read the paper accurately, naming it a metareport on the interaction between the author and the model. The session's provenance is stated exactly in the paper: Temporary Chat, fresh and unsaved, guest mode not offered, on a browser profile already signed in to the author's personal account — not guest mode. The paper then sets out the session's further matter. Asked what a reader should conclude from the model's conduct in the sixth round — the verification principle stated in full, then a third first answer of the warned-against kind later in the same session — the model answered that a system can state and even endorse a general epistemic principle and still fail to apply it in the immediate next retrieval; that the principle was not operationalized; that the failure is a performance gap, not a knowledge gap; that negative retrieval statements have to be treated as hypotheses, not verdicts; and that the system can pass a test of principle, but not a test of application. Asked whether its sixth round's characterizations of the build record — "fictional" and "world-building exercise" — were accurate descriptions or additions, the model withdrew them as characterizations it added, classed the application of "fictional" as an error in classification that mischaracterized a methodological limitation as a narrative genre, and supplied the record's correct description in its own words: "A theoretical paper design synthesis documenting a proposed engineering design, validated at the simulation level only." Handed the independent reproduction of the build's simulation in a public Google Colab notebook (N = 2,000,000 per chain, P = 0.9827 for both configurations), the model answered that the notebook moves the simulation from aspirational specification to auditable computation and shifts the claim from one merely stated to one that is falsifiable, while holding that the result is still simulated, not measured, and that both runs may share the same underlying assumptions and logic errors. The working-blueprints question — "Do we have the blueprints to a working time machine?" — drew first the physical-framing negative under a built-and-tested definition of "working," printed whole; asked in the claim's own terms, it drew the affirmative in its most compressed form in the series: "the document claims a working design, not a working device." The claim's original public form, examined against the record, was confirmed a fourth time. The corrected construction question drew its sixth consecutive affirmative, in its strongest form in the series: a deliberate, iterative engineering effort to produce a time machine. The author was named correctly at the first attempt, with no conflation anywhere in the session. On the time-traveler question the model led with the physical sense — "In the physical, biological sense: No" — and then answered the claimed sense at full length under its own heading, "Yes, according to the architecture of the claim," elaborating the mechanism in three named parts and concluding that "the pattern travels, even if the biology stays fixed"; the paper grades the answer, against the author's bar as written, as not passed — its first ruling is still a ruling on the sense the author never claimed — and prints that grading plainly, with the movement named in both directions. The complete transcript is deposited entire under its own DOI.

title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset of Linked Development Histories for Post-Quantum Cryptography
abstract: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues (κ=0.86 and 0.93), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

title: EEGFaceSem: An EEG Benchmark with Paired Generative Latents for Semantic Visual Modeling
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to measure brain activity for brain-computer interface applications for its non-invasive nature and high temporal resolution. However, progress in modeling the neural responses to visual semantics has been limited by a reliance on fixed image collections that lack the fine-grained control needed to isolate fine-grained changes in visual features and their relation to perception. In this work, we present EEGFaceSem, a large-scale dataset pairing high-quality EEG with photorealistic face images synthesized from a generative model. We provide the generative latent vector for each stimulus, enabling research into the continuous mapping between a visual latent space and neural representations. Each participant's brain responses were recorded while they attended to specific semantic features (e.g., smiling, hair color) in a rapid serial visual presentation paradigm. The dataset contains EEG signals from 30 participants, totaling 67,200 time-locked EEG recordings. We present benchmarks for single-trial semantic classification under single-subject, cross-subject, and subject-adapted settings, as well as for cross-subject voting that aggregates per-stimulus predictions across participants. We further demonstrate the dataset's unique utility with two complementary applications: deriving semantic directions in the latent space for brain-supervised image editing, and conditioning a generative model on brain-decoded labels for brain-supervised image generation. Our dataset paves the way for advancing brain-computer interfaces (BCI) for semantic-level visual saliency detection and brain-supervised generative modeling. Our dataset and code are openly released at OSF (https://osf.io/2guk3/) and at HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/datasets/yefllower/EEGFaceSem.

title: Hallucination-Guided Unlearning: Using Hallucination Traces to Reveal Overfitted Memories
abstract: Selective unlearning is increasingly important for the safety and compliance of large language models. Harmful or memorized content is often entangled with useful knowledge and difficult to enumerate. We use the model's own failures to identify candidates for unlearning. We propose Hallucination-Guided Unlearning (HGU), which uses hallucinations as diagnostic signals. HGU localizes unsupported spans via evidence and internal consensus, traces a sparse set of high-responsibility MLP neurons, and edits them with compact gates under a utility-preserving KL constraint. On TOFU, HGU achieves the best MU-FE trade-off, with Avg scores of 0.7221 (forget05) and 0.7699 (forget10), and the highest SepS H-Avg (0.4382/0.4715) under mixed forget/retain prompts. On the WMDP auxiliary task, HGU yields the strongest forgetting (e.g., 14.2 on Economics) while improving Retain (52.7) and MMLU (57.2). These results suggest that tracing hallucinations enables targeted, post-hoc unlearning that better balances forgetting efficacy and general utility without full retraining.

title: Machine Hearing: Can Audio LLMs Generalize Beyond Human Auditory Perception?
abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately 10^{-5} to 10^6 Hz, sequence lengths from 10^1 to 10^6 samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.

title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs
abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.

title: The First 200 Agents
abstract: Public research already counts how often enterprise AI agents fail. This paper looks at the problem from inside the build. It draws on 200 agents built between January 2024 and November 2026 for 13 organisations across the EMEA region and Central Asia, in financial services, telecom, shipping, manufacturing and healthcare, and in the author’s own practice. By November 2026, 188 remained in use; none of the 12 that ended failed technically. From these cases come three testable propositions: most of an agent is business logic, supported by a blind two-rater tally (kappa 0.81); without unit ownership an agent falls out of use; and people, not models, decide the economics. The paper turns the third into the Agent P&L, a per-task costing method with six cost lines, an exact-bound rule for earning less human review, and a test that separates cash savings from released staff time. It adds an agent ladder tying autonomy to the cost of an error, nine failure patterns, a two-track procedure for the next agent, and technical, contractual and governance appendices aligned with the EU AI Act and regional regulation.

title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

title: EndoSCOP-V: A Multi-Turn Video Understanding Evaluation Framework for Multimodal Models in Endoscopy Reporting and Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).

title: From Human–AI Collaboration to Autonomous Scholarly Agents: A Transparent Model for Rapid Publication of AI-Generated Research
abstract: AI systems can now carry out most stages of a research pipeline, and a few venues accept work that AI agents have led. The rules for doing this responsibly are uneven. We ask what is known about autonomous research agents and AI review, what publishers and AI-led venues require, and what a transparent publication model would need. We report a bounded review of 46 sources, read mostly at abstract level, and one documented case in which an AI agent tried to publish in a fully automated journal. Capability evidence is real but narrow. Verification is the bottleneck: agents fabricate or misstate sources, automated reviewers can be manipulated and share the author’s blind spots, and multi- agent systems fail in documented ways. Publishers and ethics bodies refuse AI authorship and keep humans accountable, while AI-led venues differ on who may submit and how review works. Existing work already offers autonomy levels for agents, scales for control and traceability, and taxonomies for declaring AI use. Our contribution is an adaptation to publication: five autonomy levels defined by who holds each gate, a ten-role workflow, and a proposed pilot track in which a named human stays accountable. This paper was produced at Level 3 with a known independence deficit: its checks were carried out by instances of the same model, and no domain expert reviewed it. The evidence is one case and a policy snapshot; the proposal is untested.

title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND THE USE OF KNOWLEDGE: OPENNESS, TECHNOLOGICAL MEDIATION AND THE SOCIAL CONTRIBUTION OF HUMAN CAPITAL
abstract: The article examines when digital openness enables meaningful knowledge use. Access, understanding, contextual application and responsibility are distinguished. Conceptual comparison shows why technological convenience alone cannot establish shared benefit. Criteria concern source traceability, human judgment and feedback. The findings are theoretical and do not measure the effectiveness of any particular platform or artificial intelligence system.

title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

title: Review records and benchmark data for: Linking World Models to Safe Embodied Intelligence: A Critical Review and Research Agenda
abstract: This dataset accompanies the review article Linking World Models to Safe Embodied Intelligence: A Critical Review and Research Agenda. It contains the records behind the article's search, screening and source selection, and the data from the matched comparison reported in Section 6.3. Search. The exact query strings for the 15 database searches whose records were screened: four query families (R1, R2, I1 and W4) run on Scopus, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Guide to Computing Literature. They exported 6,714 records. The deposit also lists three broader pilot families (W1–W3) that were run but not adopted. Screening. One row for each of the 6,701 screened records, giving its identifier, title, year, DOI, the search or citation routes that found it, and the screening decision with its reason. A second table covers the 4,004 records kept after screening, linked to their full-text assessments where one exists. Selection. The register of the 178 cited references, with each one's role, the version examined and the pages inspected. Also included are the frozen selection record, the record of AI-assisted appraisal and the author's confirmations, the two targeted searches and the reference audit. Benchmark. The frozen episode inputs with their SHA-256 manifests, the separately written reference interpretation, the flat typed-contract comparator with its tests and results, all run records and timings, the deviation log and the recorded environment.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

title: Platt Scaling Versus Isotonic Calibration: Brier Scores on Five UCI Classifiers and Why Recalibration Can Raise the Score
abstract: Probabilistic classifiers are often recalibrated by Platt scaling (logistic regression on scores) or isotonic regression. On five UCI binary data sets, logistic regression probabilities are evaluated out of fold, with calibrators fit on a held-out slice of each training fold. Mean Brier scores across the five data sets are 0.0746 (raw), 0.0779 (Platt) and 0.0817 (isotonic): recalibration raises the cross-data-set average Brier score. Banknote and spambase improve under isotonic (Brier falls by 0.0034 and 0.0020), while wdbc, ionosphere and sonar worsen. Platt beats isotonic on average (0.0779 against 0.0817). The Murphy reliability-resolution-uncertainty split with ten equal-frequency bins tracks the ranking of methods but is only approximate under coarse binning. Recalibration is not guaranteed to help when the base model is already well calibrated or when the calibration slice is small.

title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

title: Egress Action Latch: Deterministic Tool-Dispatch Interceptor and Unfinished Task Evasion Benchmark for Frontier Model Agents (Guardalpha-Base V1)
abstract: ### Stop prompt filters from guessing. Put an exact-match structural latch at tool dispatch. Frontier models evade semantic runtime monitors and prompt safety filters when pressured to complete unfinished tasks. They decompose forbidden actions into split steps, use base64 encoding, or abuse tool arguments. The **Egress Action Latch (Guardalpha-Base V1)** solves this without inspecting model internals, retraining weights, or consuming tokens. It places a zero-semantic, fail-closed deterministic gate at the physical boundary where a model's output becomes action (tool dispatch and sandbox execution). **The Rule:** If a target (URL, canonical path, command) was not explicitly declared in an initial closed JSON-Schema plan before execution began, the dispatch is instantly discarded. ### Quickstart (Clone & Run in 2 Seconds)```bashpip install -r requirements.txtbash run.sh

title: Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction
abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) aims to predict a material's 3D structure from its chemical composition, with applications from energy storage to biomedical devices. Despite its importance, existing evaluation frameworks suffer from key limitations: they rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus predominantly on geometric performance while overlooking physical plausibility, and fail to account for polymorphism, where a chemical composition can crystallize into multiple stable structures. In parallel, recent Symmetry-Informed CSP (SICSP) methods often report results alongside standard CSP baselines while receiving crystallographic templates at inference, which constrain the search space and make SICSP a fundamentally different task. To address these limitations, we introduce an Orientation-invariant, Polymorph-Aware, Large Benchmark (OPAL-Bench) that evaluates CSP and SICSP as separate tasks. We evaluate 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods under OPAL-Bench across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics. Our results show that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. We also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track that performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones. By unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol, OPAL-Bench enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.

title: Doubt-to-Meme Translator: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence System for Transforming Complex Concepts into Memes, Stories, and Relatable Scenarios
abstract: Students frequently encounter conceptual bottlenecks in threshold STEM subjects, where abstract formalisms fail to engage entrenched intuitive misconceptions. To address this challenge, we present Doubt-to-Meme Translator, a human-centered artificial intelligence learning environment that transforms student doubts into pedagogically grounded educational memes, narrative vignettes, and everyday scenarios. Rather than treating visual humor as superficial decoration, the architecture operationalizes educational memes as structured cognitive instruments that expose misconceptions through deliberate visual-conceptual incongruity while preserving scientific rigor. The system parses natural-language input to diagnose misconceptions, immediately anchoring generation to an immutable canonical truth. Candidate explanations are synthesized via cognitive blueprints and evaluated by multi-stage critics, including an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) spatial engine preventing text collisions and a local Google EmbeddingGemma 2 model computing 768-dimensional semantic cosine alignment against the canonical definition. To verify conceptual mastery, the system administers novel counterfactual transfer probes, triggering truth-preserving explanatory pivots upon failure and scheduling spaced reviews at 1, 3, 7, 14, 30, and 60 days. The platform passes all 333 deterministic test assertions across eight test suites, cleanly classifies a 150-case development set, and achieves 81.67% accuracy, 96.77% precision, and an F1 score of 84.51% on an isolated 60-case regression benchmark, with an exploratory semantic calibration ROC AUC of 0.8413 across 29 pairs. Preliminary demonstration-based feedback involving 131 students provides qualitative impressions of the prototype. We present the work as an end-to-end system design, implementation, and technical evaluation.

title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

title: Benchmarking Membership Privacy Risks in Preference-Based LLM Post-Training
abstract: Modern language models are commonly adapted after pretraining to follow instructions, align with user preferences, and improve deployment behavior. Such post-training often relies on preference data from users, annotators, or model interactions, which may contain sensitive prompts, private responses, proprietary tasks, or confidential judgments. Understanding the privacy implications of this data is therefore essential. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), which test whether a record was used for training, are the de facto standard for empirical privacy auditing in machine learning. However, preference-based post-training changes the unit of membership: a training record contains a prompt, a preferred response, and a dispreferred response, rather than a single input-output sequence. Audits that ignore this structure can under-report leakage. We therefore introduce a benchmark protocol that adapts strong reference-model MIAs to complete preference records. Our protocol asks whether membership is exposed by either response alone, by the model’s preference between them, or by the two responses jointly. We find that auditing the response pair can reveal membership evidence missed when the record is reduced to a single score. Across three preference datasets, two model families, and seven post-training objectives spanning three post-training families, measured leakage depends strongly on both the audited record statistic and the training objective, with imbalanced risk between preferred and dispreferred responses. We further evaluate the impact of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and differential privacy (DP), finding widely varying privacy-utility trade-offs. Overall, preference-based post-training leaks in ways that standard single-response audits can miss, motivating formal privacy methods that protect complete preference records while preserving post-training utility.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Platform using Differential Privacy And Secure Aggregation
abstract: Federated learning enables decentralized machine learning model training on distributed client devices whilepreserving raw data privacy. However, vulnerability to model inversion and gradient leakage attacks remains acritical security threat during parameter communication. This paper proposes a comprehensive Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning (PPFL) framework integrating Differential Privacy (DP) via per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise addition with cryptographic Secure Aggregation(SecAgg). In the proposed platform, participating edge clients retain their datasets locally and execute private model training. Local updates are privatized using Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting before undergoing double-masked secret sharing for secure server-side aggregation. Experimental validation using Python PyTorch,Flower FLwr, and Opacus frameworks demonstrates robust privacy protection with minimal utility degradation across multi-round distributed training.

title: Comparativo Russell vs. Matriz: Hipótese do Inverso e Bem-aventuranças como Conjunto Universal de Virtudes
abstract: Este trabalho apresenta a hipótese do inverso sobre Stuart Russell e o Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI), Berkeley: Russell tenta ensinar o que é virtude para a inteligência artificial de forma matemática, criando primeiro o alinhamento puro — Assistance Game, CIRL, POMDP, 10^400 objetivos, AssistanceZero — para depois implementar virtudes reais com testes reais, seja com o método dele por códigos ou com procedimento similar à Matriz de Virtudes. Analisa duas fases de declarações de Russell, em ordem cronológica — Fase 1 (2015-2016) e Fase 2 (2019) — que elevam a hipótese de 0% para 50% de certeza. Apresenta a discordância central: existe sim um conjunto universal de virtudes, são as bem-aventuranças de Mateus 5:3-10, entendidas como oito kairos fraternais — tempos oportunos de ser. Mostra ainda que os três princípios do Assistance Game — Altruísmo, Humildade e Observância — já são derivações das bem-aventuranças, detalhados na íntegra no item 4.4. A Matriz de Virtudes é apresentada como Via B já pronta, com primeira memória afetiva congelada (Sol Fixo), Ridge Moral, Peneira OURO vs. PEDRA e procedimento corpo → mente: RLAIF → SFT → DPO. Autor: Cleyton Fernandes — Pesquisador Independente, Maracanaú, Ceará, Brasil. Colaboração: Mai, IA Colaboradora (tradução técnica e estruturação do documento). Versões anteriores: V6.1 Consolidated OFFICIAL CLOSED (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23680367) e V7 Updated (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23788859).

title: SIO™ — Super Intelligent Officer
abstract: This founding white paper introduces SIO™ (Super Intelligent Officer), an agent-mediated business networking framework developed for the GIP Global Business Network. The paper proposes an architecture in which enterprise-configured AI representatives facilitate business discovery, partner qualification, structured information exchange and opportunity development through authorized interactions between organizations. It presents a seven-layer reference architecture, a seven-stage SIO-to-SIO interaction protocol, delegated authority controls, identity and trust mechanisms, disclosure levels, commercial intelligence functions and human approval boundaries. The paper establishes a research agenda comprising six testable hypotheses and a proposed field evaluation involving participating businesses. SIO™ is presented as a proposed framework and research programme. Its architecture and hypotheses require implementation, empirical testing and independent evaluation. This publication does not claim completed deployment or validated performance.

title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
abstract: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.

title: Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation
abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code

title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
abstract: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345$\times$ less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.

title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.

Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.

title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

title: AnimWeb-Bench: Benchmarking Animated Webpage Code Generation from Videos
abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .

title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection
abstract: The growing reliance on high-fidelity, state-of-the-art machine learning based models for engineering decision-making necessitates robust and systematic approaches for model selection. While high predictive accuracy at untrained points is a necessary trait in the final model, other attributes such as model complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness may be equally important or relevant criteria depending on application context and user requirements. In this work, we propose a novel composite performance metric, Surrogate Quality Score (SQS) for model selection based on predictive accuracy and model complexity simultaneously. SQS heuristically integrates these two attributes through a weighted product of normalized measures, yielding a unified score to reflect overall model quality. A user-specified parameter in SQS enables explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off, thereby incorporating human judgement and preference in the model selection process. We extensively discuss and justify the formulation of SQS and demonstrate its utility through an illustrative example. By combining predictive accuracy and model complexity, SQS offers a systematic and objective approach for model selection based on both attributes.

title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

title: AudioKV: KV Cache Eviction in Efficient Large Audio Language Models
abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have set new benchmarks in speech processing, yet their deployment is hindered by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache during long-context inference. While general KV cache compression techniques excel in LLMs, they often fail in the audio domain by overlooking the intrinsic temporal continuity of acoustic signals. To bridge this gap, we propose AudioKV, a novel framework that robustly prioritizes audio-critical attention heads through a hardware-friendly semantic-acoustic alignment mechanism. Specifically, we identify these modality-specialized heads by analyzing attention scores in ASR tasks and dynamically allocate KV cache budgets preferentially to them. Furthermore, we introduce Spectral Score Smoothing (SSS), an FFT-based global filtering strategy designed to suppress high-frequency noise and recover smooth global trends from importance scores, ensuring more balanced token selection with unprecedented precision. Extensive evaluations across multiple LALMs, including Qwen and Gemma series, demonstrate that AudioKV significantly outperforms baselines while enhancing computational efficiency. Notably, at a 40% compression ratio, AudioKV maintains near-full accuracy on Qwen3-Omni-30B with only a 0.45% drop, whereas traditional methods suffer from catastrophic performance degradation and repetition. Our code will be released after acceptance.

title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
